title: Germans astonished by Black Americans; the Gene Cedric incident
summary: At the Darmstader Hoff, Gene Cedric scares an inquisitive German woman reading his letter, and Wooding reflects that Germans thought Africans were brought to America temporarily.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Now we was all staying at -- we lived at a place called Darmstader Hoff. This all happened in East Berlin, on Friederich-strasse. And as we were standing outside talking, one of the boys, Gene Cedric -- he was tenor saxophone, later on became very popular over here with Fats Waller and some other -- anyhow, he was reading a letter from St. Louis. And it was telling him about -- so the guys all gathered around him and said, 'Gee, you got a letter.' So this old German woman come up too, and she stood right there and was reading over his shoulder. Because the Germans are very inquisitive people. They're a fine race of people and they are well educated, but they're specialists. If a man is a specialist at making cups, he don't know how to make saucers. If he's a doctor, he specializes in one type. If he's the heart man -- they're not general practitioners at nothing. They specialize, and if they specialize at making pianos, he can make the hell out of a piano, but he can't do nothing with a clarinet. Nothing else. He just do whatever he -- they
were specialists in those days, they were not generalists.

So now, when this little woman come up and was looking over Gene's shoulder, one fellow said to Gene, "Gene, you've got company." And Gene says, "I see her." And she was there reading his letter, so Gene turned around and said, "Arrrrrrrr", like that, and she stood right there and urinated all over herself.
Yeah, she was scared. They still believed that we only stayed in America for a little while. That we were brought here until we reached a certain age, and then were taken back to Africa.

They didn't believe we stayed here and was reared, been here since 1620. They didn't believe that. And you didn't know anything. And just like a donkey. They couldn't understand how we learned to blow those horns. We had a trombone player that they swore that he was singing through his horn.

Cause see, Germans play more a la Wagner. (sings a few bars of Wagner) And especially in those days, because it's a very harsh race. They don't have the nice beautiful German, like in Munich and Vienna has. See, Germany is not the

fine arts. The mechanical arts. They excel in things like that. But in the fine arts, like medicine and art and music. That's the reason why the great German composers eventually went to -- like Brahms and all, went to Vienna to live. Because they had the smoothness, the Viennese had the smoothness, while the Germans were -- (hup, hup.) but they were great people. They even had that in the voice,
